title: The two Dals
hook: the Khalsa organized into the elders' army and the young army

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nawab Kapur Singh, the man with the fan who was given a governor's title. Your line was the humble nawab. Who did you cool down? Today, what the humble nawab built. Day eight hundred fifty-three.

Here is a tension that turns up in families, in teams, in congregations. The young want to move. The old want to keep. The young say: you're too careful. The old say: you're too quick. Sometimes one side wins and the other drifts away. The Khalsa, in its hard century, had both kinds of Sikh in its ranks, with real lives at stake. And tradition says that under Nawab Kapur Singh each was given a name and a job. Today: the two Dals.
screen: `THE YOUNG WANT TO MOVE.` → `THE OLD WANT TO KEEP.` → `A NAME AND A JOB FOR EACH.`

segments.voice: Dal means a host, an army, a body of people moving together. Tradition says that under Nawab Kapur Singh the Khalsa was organized into two of them. The Budha Dal, the army of the elders. And the Taruna Dal, the army of the young. Each had its own work. The tellings say the Budha Dal, the older Sikhs, looked after the holy places and the steady life of the community, and gave counsel. The Taruna Dal, the younger riders, took on the fast, dangerous work of defense, moving where they were needed. Neither was the junior partner. The elders were not pushed aside as too slow. The young were not held back as too reckless. In the tellings, they were separate, but not apart. Tradition says that when the Khalsa gathered at Amritsar, both Dals came together, sat in the same sangat, and made decisions as one. The young had the elders' memory. The elders had the young's strength. And over both stood a shared allegiance: not to a Dal, but to the Guru's way. Tradition says the Taruna Dal later grew and was divided into smaller bands, and those bands, in time, became the seeds of something bigger. But today the point is simpler. A community needs its grandparents and its teenagers. It needs the ones who remember why and the ones who can still run. The two Dals are a picture of how not to waste either.
screen: `DAL: AN ARMY, A HOST.` · `BUDHA DAL: THE ELDERS.` · `TARUNA DAL: THE YOUNG.` · `SEPARATE, BUT NOT APART.` · then, large: `OLD AND YOUNG TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect both elders and youth. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind one person in your life who is a good deal older than you. Let one thing they know, that you don't, come to mind. Then bring to mind one person a good deal younger. Let one thing they can do, that you can't anymore, or never could, come to mind. Hold the two of them side by side for a while. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The two Dals. The Budha Dal of the elders and the Taruna Dal of the young, two bodies of the Khalsa with different work and one shared sangat. Today's word.
Your line: old and young together. Today, ask one older person for their advice, and ask one younger person to show you something. Day eight hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Budha Dal and Taruna Dal as the Khalsa's organization under Nawab Kapur Singh, and Nihang Sikh groups today still carry the name Budha Dal.

original.note: Gurmukhi: dal, a host or army; Budha Dal, the elders, and Taruna Dal, the young.

trapdoor: what you thought: two political parties.
what it means: the Khalsa split its work between an elders' army and a young army, and gathered them in one sangat.
what a scholar hears: tradition credits Nawab Kapur Singh with the Budha Dal and Taruna Dal, and says the Taruna Dal was later divided into smaller bands.

notes: The age line between the Dals (often given as forty) and the number of jathas the Taruna Dal was divided into (often five) are omitted under the claims rule.
The division of work (Budha Dal: holy places and counsel; Taruna Dal: defense) is told as 'the tellings say'; confirm.
'Those bands, in time, became the seeds of something bigger' alludes to the later misls without naming them, to avoid teaching ahead. Confirm.
Glosses: dal = host/army, budha = old, taruna = young; these are meanings, not etymologies. Confirm.
howItsDone: Nihang groups still carrying the name Budha Dal; confirm phrasing.
Editor pass: stock line 'here is the wise part' cut; the joint gatherings at Amritsar now attributed to tradition.

Audit (fresh reviewer): the hook said the Khalsa 'faced exactly this' quarrel and that Kapur Singh 'answered it'; the sources give the organization, not a generational dispute behind it. Hook softened to what tradition says; 'separate, but not apart' attributed to the tellings. The fork's setup still imagines a pull between young and old; a Keeper may prefer a neutral setup.
